title: How SETI Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain SETI (Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence), timed to Science Channel's Are We Alone? Month. They cover the Wow! signal of 1977 (mis-stated as August fifty seven in the transcript), the SETI Institute's origins with Frank Drake and the Drake equation, the three main challenges (vast sky, choice of radio frequency including the "water hole" and prime-number ideas, and limited equipment), search projects like Project Phoenix, SERENDIP, the Allen Telescope Array, and SETI@home, the Fermi paradox, the protocol for announcing a detected signal, and whether humans should send messages. The episode closes with live show announcements for South by Southwest in Austin, a TV pilot for Science Channel, and listener mail about wrestling (razor blades for blading, WWE, TNA, Ring of Honor).

segments.title: Opening banter and Are We Alone Month
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter, a personal announcement, and introduce the topic of aliens, tied to Science Channel's Are We Alone? Month and the SETI topic.

segments.title: The Wow! signal
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh describe the Wow! signal, a 72-second narrowband radio burst recorded in 1977 at Ohio State's Big Ear radio telescope, which was never detected again and was named after Jerry Ehman's note on the printout. The transcript gives the date as August fifty seven.

segments.title: Origins of SETI and the Drake equation
segments.summary: SETI's origins in the intellectual push to search for alien life, including Morrison and Cocconi's Nature paper and Frank Drake's founding of the search. The hosts walk through the Drake equation's factors, which yield anywhere from one to billions of communicative civilizations.

segments.title: Three challenges: sky, frequency, and equipment
segments.summary: The hosts outline SETI's three main challenges: the large sky (wide-field versus targeted searches), choosing among billions of radio frequencies, and limited telescope time and funding. They explain the water hole band and the idea that prime-number frequencies might be used.

segments.title: Search projects: Phoenix, SERENDIP, Allen Telescope Array, SETI@home
segments.summary: Projects include Project Phoenix, which rents time on radio telescopes including Arecibo and Green Bank, and SERENDIP, which piggybacks on other observations. The hosts describe using interferometry with backyard satellite dishes and the SETI@home screen saver that distributes data processing. The Allen Telescope Array, funded by Paul Allen, has been short on money and is partly operating on a skeleton crew.

segments.title: Fermi paradox and signal detection protocols
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Fermi paradox and SETI's view that life is probably out there. They then describe the protocol after a signal is detected: verifying it by moving the telescope, checking other sources, and notifying the astronomical community, the UN, and the public. They say SETI doesn't believe in a secret alien presence at Roswell.

segments.title: Sending messages, future of SETI, and sign-off mentions
segments.summary: The hosts note that Earth has been unintentionally broadcasting for decades and that SETI is passive, though symbolic messages like the Arecibo message and plaques on Pioneer and Voyager probes were sent. They discuss optical SETI as a future direction and encourage listeners to try SETI@home.

segments.title: Live show announcements
segments.summary: Hosts announce live podcasts at South by Southwest in Austin, a public variety show at Fado Irish Pub, and a Science Channel TV pilot.

segments.title: Listener mail on wrestling
segments.summary: Listener Zack corrects the hosts on wrestling: wrestlers usually use razor blades for blading rather than fake blood packs, and he lists the major U.S. promotions WWE, TNA, and Ring of Honor, plus independent leagues.
